This book appealed because both my wife and I are dealing with various and new forms of pain. We also expect that dealing with pain in one form or another will be a reasonably constant part of the rest of our lives.

It's a lovely explainer, targeted at (what else) getting AI to act more like a librarian and ferret out what your question(s) really mean. It's a powerful technique and will almost certainly give you much better results than the typical "ask-answer-walk-away" approach we so often use with both search and AI.

> Search engines and chatbots answer what we give them directly, without asking what we meant. A chatbot can take the librarian's side of the interview, though, if we ask it to question us first.

Here's the thing: this is about so much more than search or AI. It's a mindset that, once adopted, lets you question yourself. Regardless of what tool you're using, or whether you're using any tool at all, the process of refining and clarifying just gets better answers.

The essay includes a prompt you can feed to your friendly neighborhood chatbot, of course, but structuring your own approach along the same lines is perhaps the most valuable takeaway of all.

Do this: Question yourself.

Again, ignore the twenty-one and thirty. Replace them with <your age> and <your age + 10>.

The advice Westenberg offers is ageless: become good at a skill; learn to sell; learn to write; build equity; learn to use AI tools; save and invest; take care of your health; don't date dickheads; be intentional with friendships; pick your location wisely; start asking for what you want; share your work; build a body of work; learn to recover quickly; take risks while you can; take back your attention; spend time with your parents; design your own life. item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 3 of 7.

Ness Letters: The Comfort Paradox – Anne-Laure Le Cunff – (Ness Labs)

We live in amazing times. So much more is possible, and so much is being done for us; it's truly incredible. And yet almost everything we now see as "amazing" and "incredible" will someday, no doubt, be seen as normal and anything but noteworthy. And the results? The results will have less perceived value simply because they'll be considered mundane.

The argument here is that there's value in purposely adding difficulty to some of our tasks.

> We spend our lives trying to make everything easier, yet some of the things that make life worth living require difficulty.

I think the most obvious example right now might be how we connect with each other. It's trivial to message anyone anywhere on the planet and get a response in seconds. I won't say that this devalues the relationship, but it certainly makes it less "special" than a long-distance conversation might have been in the past. I'm also not saying that's an example of something we should purposely make more difficult. Far from it. But it is a tangible example of how ease can lead us to take for granted things that perhaps we should value more.

Do this: Consider whether some of the easy things in your life warrant a little more attention.

#comfort
